title: Checking People In
sub: Seeing who came, and marking them arrived
detail: There is no guest-list table: each event row holds its guest list as one JSON text, rsvp. The organiser opens it from the event's details and taps a person to mark them arrived, which rewrites the whole text.

explain.body:
Explorify is a campus events app: student organisations post events, and students join them from their phones. On the night, the organisation wants to know who actually came, so an organiser opens the event and ticks people off as they arrive.

Most apps keep a guest list as a table of its own, one row per guest. Explorify does not: each event's row in the database has one text column, `rsvp`, holding the whole guest list as a single piece of JSON (a text format for nested data). Joining, cancelling and checking in all read that text, change it, and write all of it back.

That design is why this part has a problem worth knowing before you touch it: when two people change the list at nearly the same moment, the later write wins and the earlier change is lost.

issues.title: Checking someone in can erase newer RSVPs
issues.detail: The Attendees screen does not use the copy the details page just fetched. The first tap writes back a guest list loaded when the Ongoing list was opened, so anyone who joined or changed their booking since is silently removed.

children.title: What An RSVP Holds
children.sub: One entry per student, in one text
children.detail: Each student who joins gets one entry in the event's rsvp text, keyed by their user id. The join drawer writes the entry; the organiser's tap only adds checkedIn.

explain.body:
Every student who joins gets one entry in the event's guest-list text. The entry is filed under the student's user id, the random code the app gave their account, so joining a second time replaces the old entry rather than adding another.

An entry holds what the student typed when joining: their name, how to reach them, how many people they are bringing, and any food needs. The organiser's check-in tap only ever adds one more field to it, `checkedIn`, true or false.

children.sub: The join drawer adds one student's entry
children.detail: The drawer reads the event's `rsvp` text, sets the entry under the student's id, and writes the whole text back. `Other` opens a text box whose words are stored one per comma.

explain.body:
When a student taps Join, a drawer slides up asking for their name, how to reach them, party size and food needs. Saving it does three things in order: fetch the event's current guest-list text, add or replace this student's entry in it, and save the whole text back.

Because the whole text is saved, anything that changed between the fetch and the save is overwritten.

children.title: The Student Feed
children.sub: Every published event on the student's campus
children.detail: The feed loads every published event on the student's campus with `select("*")`, so each event's `rsvp` text comes with it.

explain.body:
A student's home screen, the feed, shows every published event on their campus. To build it, the app asks the database for every column of those events, and one of those columns is the guest-list text.

So each student's phone quietly downloads the names, emails and food needs of everyone who joined every event on campus, though the feed never shows them.

children.title: Attendee List Screen
children.sub: Everyone who joined, and their dietary needs
children.detail: A tally of dietary needs, then one row per booking from the event's rsvp text. Tapping a row checks that person in, or out again.

explain.body:
The full attendee list is the screen an organiser holds at the door. At the top, a tally of food needs helps whoever orders the food; below it, one row per booking. A booking is one student's entry, and it can bring more than one person.

Tapping a row marks that booking arrived with a green tick; tapping again takes the tick away.

issues.title: Pictures can belong to someone else
issues.detail: Row N takes the Nth picture from the details page, whose list comes back from the database in its own order and only for students who still have a profile. Faces can sit next to the wrong names, and if this screen's copy has more people than that list — someone cancelled, or deleted their account — the screen crashes on the extra row.

issues.title: Dietary counts are per booking, not per person
issues.detail: Maya's party of two counts once under Vegan, the same as a party of one. An organiser ordering food from these numbers can only guess how many plates each need applies to.

children.title: Marking Someone Arrived
children.sub: One tap rewrites the whole guest list
children.unsure: Whether the database lets one organisation write another organisation's event depends on its row-level security rules, which live in the Supabase dashboard and not in this repository.
children.detail: A tap flips one person's checkedIn flag and writes the whole guest list back, without reading it first. The copy it writes can be as old as the Ongoing list, so newer RSVPs are erased.

explain.body:
Checking someone in should change one thing: that person's tick. But the guest list is one text, so the app sets the tick in its own copy of the text and saves the whole copy back.

That copy is whatever the screen was handed when the organiser opened it, possibly minutes ago. If a student joined since then, the saved copy does not include them and they vanish from the list. The sequence on this page shows it happening with two students, Maya and Leo.

issues.title: A tap overwrites newer RSVPs
issues.detail: The update writes the screen's copy of the whole guest list without reading the current one. Anyone who joined, cancelled or changed their party since the copy was taken is reverted — joiners disappear from the event, though their own app still says they joined.

issues.title: Other organisations' guest lists are tappable
issues.detail: From the organisation's search, any campus event opens the same details and Attendees screens, and the tap updates the event by id alone. Unless the database's own rules refuse it, one organisation can check people in — or erase RSVPs — at another's event.
